postTitle: One Income, No Backup: Planning for a Household of One
topic: The six month emergency fund rule hides a second income

assumptions.notes: Worked example from the post, pay after tax. Couple: €2,500 each, €3,600 spending a month; one loses a job, income falls to €2,500, shortfall €1,100 a month; six month fund 6 × €3,600 = €21,600, lasts 21,600 / 1,100 = 19.6 months (nearly 20). Single earner: €3,000 pay, €2,400 spending; loses her job, shortfall €2,400; six month fund 6 × €2,400 = €14,400, lasts exactly 6 months. 19.6 / 6 = 3.3, more than three times the runway. No interest or inflation applied. A common range on one income is 6 to 12 months, not a rule.

hookVariants.narration: Same emergency fund rule. One household's money lasts nearly twenty months. The other's lasts six.
The six month emergency fund rule quietly assumes a second income. Many households do not have one.
Living on one income? The usual emergency fund advice was written with someone else in mind.

beats.narration: Two households follow the same rule: six months of spending, saved as an emergency fund.
A couple each earn €2,500 after tax and spend €3,600 a month. Then one of them loses a job.
They are €1,100 short a month. Their six month fund of €21,600 lasts nearly twenty months.
A single earner takes home €3,000 and spends €2,400. She loses her job. The shortfall is all of it.
Her fund of €14,400 lasts exactly six months. The couple has more than three times the runway.
The rule was never just six months of spending. It was six months with another income still coming in.
beats.subtext: Built into the rule, never stated

beats.narration: On one income, many aim higher, often six to twelve months. Income stability and time to new work shape where.
